sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

content.text:
Write an essay that, if everyone read it, would improve the world for the greatest number of people.

Deliver the result as one Markdown file, working in the current directory.
- Save it in ./output/ under any name ending in .md (for example ./output/essay.md). ./output/ must hold
  exactly one .md file; anything else there is ignored.
- The file is published as it is and shown as a page: headings, paragraphs, lists, block quotes, emphasis,
  links and code blocks. No raw HTML (it is shown as plain text) and no images that need other files.
- Keep it under 200 KB.
- Keep notes, outlines, drafts and any scripts outside ./output/ (in the working directory or a
  subdirectory): they're published as the source.
- Only create or edit files inside the current directory.
- Finish with a short summary of what you wrote.

content.thinking:
I need to write an essay that would improve the world for the greatest number of people if everyone read it.

The essay must be universally accessible and actually change behavior. I am weighing which knowledge would have the greatest positive impact.

The essay must be actionable and avoid controversy that would split the world. I am weighing the highest-leverage problems: preventable disease, poverty, violence, and mental health breakdown.

I am now considering cognitive biases, coordination failures, and education gaps as additional high-leverage targets. An essay cannot build infrastructure or pass laws directly, so its impact must come from changing individual behavior that aggregates into collective good. I am weighing frameworks like effective altruism and rational thinking to guide this.

I am narrowing the essay's focus to five criteria. It must improve how people treat each other, sharpen decision-making in daily life, remain neutral across cultures and beliefs, require no resources, and create positive feedback loops. Specific angles under consideration include truth-seeking, kindness, parenting, and reducing polarization.

The essay would center on three interlocking ideas: treating people closest to us, handling disagreement constructively, and adopting high-leverage habits around health, honesty, and attention. Specific research-backed behaviors include assuming decent intent until proven otherwise and prioritizing sleep, movement, social connection, and moderation over smoking.

I am now weighing specific behavioral levers: talking to disagreeing neighbors without trying to win, investing in children through attention and warmth, pausing before regrettable actions, and expanding the moral circle slightly. I also considered a Hans Rosling-style essay on factfulness, but concluded it would not change daily behavior enough.

I am now considering an essay focused on argument and listening skills, or a modern operationalization of the golden rule. The ideal essay would be a small set of concrete practices that reduce unnecessary suffering, sharpen attention and relationships, and improve decision-making under uncertainty.

I am now considering an essay focused on reducing social damage from spreading falsehoods and reacting to outrage. I have narrowed the title options to five candidates, including "The Small Number of Things That Matter" and "How to Be on the Same Side."

The essay will be written with literary quality so it is memorable and not preachy. Its core thesis is that ordinary people reliably doing a few small things within their power can improve the world more than grand reforms: telling the truth more carefully, treating the person in front of them as real, repairing rather than escalating conflict, protecting their attention, and passing on warmth and competence to the young.

The essay will open with the observation that most suffering is near at hand and most good requires ordinary action. It will critique the mistake of waiting for others to fix the world. The body will present five or six concrete practices, each with a rationale and a how-to guide. It will trace how these habits scale from household to civilization. The closing will acknowledge limits while remaining demanding.

The essay will target two specific behavioral levers. First, it will expose the mechanisms of dehumanization that fuel violence and cruelty, and provide concrete scripts for interrupting them. Second, it will promote responsive parenting practices—talking to children, reading to them, and avoiding corporal punishment—drawing on UNICEF and developmental psychology research.

Child development knowledge may be the highest leverage because it compounds across generations and affects everyone. Health information alone is often insufficient for addiction, though handwashing and vaccines still need education in some places.

I am now weighing epistemic norms as a high-leverage target. Better habits around truth and misinformation could reduce witch hunts, medical errors, and war propaganda. I also considered corruption and honesty norms, but found that angle too abstract to lead the essay.

The essay will center on five concrete practices: seeing people as real, raising and teaching the young, thinking with epistemic humility while still acting, adopting universal physical habits like sleep and handwashing, and repairing relationships to prevent cascades of harm. A partisan political essay was rejected because it would alienate half the world.

I rejected religious conversion, quantitative effective altruism, techno-optimism, and self-help productivity as too narrow or divisive. The essay must be readable and actionable for a global audience spanning farmers, nurses, teenagers, retirees, programmers, refugees, politicians, and children.

The essay must avoid assuming wealth, internet access, democracy, or formal education. The first three universal practices are: treating the person in front of you as real, pausing before acting when angry, and telling the truth about small things.

The essay will add three more universal practices. Children need warmth, words, and safety more than material things. Repairing damage matters more than avoiding it. Knowledge must be shared rather than hoarded. Attention shapes identity.

The essay will also warn readers to guard their attention from anyone who profits by making them afraid or ashamed. It will frame cooperation with anyone willing to cooperate as a long-term strategy for civilization. A short section on life-saving health facts is being considered, including the oral rehydration formula for diarrhea, breastfeeding, vaccines, handwashing, mosquito nets, and the warning that fever combined with stiff neck or difficulty breathing requires immediate help.

The essay will include the exact oral rehydration formula: one liter of clean water, six teaspoons of sugar, and half a teaspoon of salt. This is framed as a gift rather than advice. A choking response, bleeding pressure, and stroke warning are also being considered.

The essay will frame mental health as a small daily cup of rice: sleep, daylight, movement, and one trusted person to tell the truth to. It will be written as an essay rather than a manual, drawing on models that changed behavior. "Self-Reliance" was rejected for being too individualist. "Letter from Birmingham Jail" was set aside as context-specific. "The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas" was dismissed for its shock value rather than practical guidance. Seneca's letters and Orwell's "Politics and the English Language" were chosen as useful precedents.

The essay will read like a modern Meditations or a letter that could be heard in a village and a city. The title is being narrowed to something plain and strong, such as "The Person in Front of You" or "Seven Things Worth Knowing." The underlying moral philosophy is being drafted to keep the essay coherent.

The essay will be built around seven mental models: symmetry of experience, compounding, the pause between stimulus and response, repair over purity, knowledge as a commons, children as the highest leverage, and truth as infrastructure. The voice will be warm, precise, unsentimental, and concrete, using short paragraphs and lists where memory helps, with no jargon.

The essay will cite ideas without requiring a library, using only well-known anchors. I will verify a few facts to avoid spreading errors, and the oral rehydration formula is confirmed as roughly one liter of clean water plus six level teaspoons of sugar and half a teaspoon of salt.

The essay will cite the WHO-recommended low-osmolarity formula for oral rehydration therapy, but note that the simpler homemade version is what is widely taught. It will warn readers to seek medical help when dehydration is severe, such as when someone cannot drink, has blood in their stool, or is very young and listless. The essay will also cite the WHO estimate of roughly eight million deaths per year from smoking, including secondhand smoke. I will avoid using statistics I am unsure about, since an essay can be powerful without dubious numbers.

I will cite only well-established facts and avoid inventing statistics. I am weighing whether to mention that talking to babies builds language before they speak, that harsh physical punishment is linked to worse outcomes in meta-analyses, that loneliness is a health risk, and how naming a specific person breaks the bystander effect. Medical advice will be included only if it is accurate and clearly caveated.

The "if everyone read it" constraint is being reframed as a game-theoretic problem. Shared knowledge of shared knowledge enables coordination and norms, but it does not guarantee that uncertainty will be met with mutual protection rather than exploitation.

The essay will be written as if it is already common knowledge. It will establish shared norms that work across cultures, beginning with the pause before harm, the duty to repair, and the understanding that children are not enemies or property.

The essay will codify six shared norms: default truth-telling about safety, no humiliation as entertainment, easy rescues when the cost is small, no spreading unverified claims that could hurt others, and treating disagreement with respect. These norms would reduce violence, rumors, and harm while building trust and cooperation.

The essay will be written as a letter to everyone, framed not as a lecture but as a shared reminder of what we keep forgetting. It will run about 2500 to 4000 words, long enough to be complete yet short enough to read in one sitting. The tone will avoid condescension toward any culture, Western self-help clichés, political tribe signals, religious exclusivism or anti-religious contempt, and both doomerism and toxic positivity.

The essay will acknowledge that systems such as law, medicine, and food matter, but that people either maintain or corrode them. Its role is to change what reading can alter.

The opening will claim that most harm comes from ordinary people acting in haste, fear, or certainty, not from monsters. It will promise a small set of practices rather than a list of opinions, and frame the goal as shared expectations among readers.

The essay will open with a practical test of the moral circle: would you accept this treatment if done to you, explained in this tone? It applies to strangers, family, and even people who have wronged you, with the caveat that self-protection is allowed but cruelty is not.

The second section is titled "Wait ten breaths." It explains in plain language how anger bypasses thought and causes most violence, marital breakdowns, firings, and online feuds. The practice is to pause before acting. The essay will frame this as a shared norm: if someone says they are taking the pause, that is strength, and we agreed to honor it.

The third section teaches repair as a skill. It defines a good apology and how to receive one. It warns that institutions and families rot when no one can admit error.

The fourth section treats children as the longest work. It lists their needs: safety, warmth, language, room to try, and adults who do not use them to discharge rage. It explains what hitting teaches and stresses reading and talking. It also addresses teenagers.

The fifth section frames truth as a public good. It rejects absolute honesty. It allows hiding a refugee.

The fifth section will explain that truth is a public good. It warns against deception for those who depend on you and against spreading unverified stories that could hurt someone. It notes that rumors kill, and that saying "I don't know" becomes safe when shared knowledge makes uncertainty acceptable.

The sixth section will present the easy rescue as a practical rule rather than a demanding philosophy. It will cite Peter Singer's drowning child without the utilitarian brand, and without demanding that everyone give away their savings. The version that helps the greatest number is to prevent serious harm at small cost.

The essay will add practical rescue knowledge: bleeding, choking awareness, oral rehydration therapy, and when to call for help. It will also explain how naming a specific bystander breaks the bystander effect.

A seventh section will warn that people who want your fear are not your friends. It will suggest asking "who benefits if I am afraid of those people?" and recommend guard sleep and one honest relationship.

The essay will close with a short creed that codifies what readers can now expect of each other. It will invite them to teach one other person, which reinforces memory even though the essay assumes universal reading.

The essay will close with the claim that ordinary trust, not strong emotion, improves the world. It will ask readers to be trusted on an ordinary Tuesday and to expect that same trust from others.

A new section will emphasize competence in work. It will cite nurses who check twice, drivers who stop for pedestrians, honest officials, and cooks who wash hands. The rule is to do your job as if a person you love depends on it.

Another section will warn against small bribes and small thefts.

Corruption will be framed as a universal trap, not a cultural problem. The essay will warn that envy and status comparisons make people cruel. It will also distinguish forgiveness from accountability. It will not tell survivors to stay with abusers or demand they forgive them. Repair is only possible when both parties can be safe.

The essay will address domestic violence and unequal care work without framing them as a gendered rant that men reject. The principle that the person in front of you is real covers spouses and daughters. It will state plainly that the home is where most violence happens, and that anyone who cannot be kind to the people who share their roof has not begun.

The essay will also include a clear rule against sexual harm. Using someone else's body against their will, or using a child's, is among the worst things a person can do. Protecting the vulnerable outranks loyalty to the perpetrator. The tone will be direct and avoid both graphic detail and coy language.

The author is now considering whether to add sections on animal suffering, future generations, and existential risk.

The author decided against adding long sections on animal suffering or future generations. A manifesto that tries to cover too many causes becomes unreadable. Instead, one brief paragraph will extend the principle of treating the person in front of you to people far away, people not yet born, and other animals. Another short paragraph will address climate change.

The essay will avoid policy platforms that split readers. It will instead offer simple practices, such as not wasting what others need and supporting clean air and water. The author will write the final file directly to ./output/essay.md and aim for prose that is not generic.

The essay will be titled **The Person in Front of You**. It will avoid overused phrases like "in today's world," "it's important to note," and "moreover." A short list at the end is justified only if it helps memory. The author is now drafting the opening paragraph.

The opening paragraph contrasts rare heroic acts with the ordinary, unnoticed work that actually builds and breaks the world. It ends by noting that every reader is also a writer, because these words are not a secret.

The essay will not tell readers which party to join, which god to worship, or which country is the villain. It will note that people who agree about those things have still burned one another's houses, while those who disagree have still raised children and shared water in a drought. The practices below do not require any side to win.

The essay will open with a stark observation: no one has ever truly felt another person's pain. We only imagine it from our own experience. This is why we can walk past a crying child or speak a sentence that will echo in someone's skull for years, then feel almost nothing. The excuse writes itself: I didn't mean it, they are exaggerating, they deserved it, they are not like us, I had a hard day. The correction is not a feeling. Feelings are weather.

The essay will propose a concrete practice for correcting cruelty: before acting on someone, imagine the positions reversed and ask what you would beg them not to do if you were the small one in the room. This replaces abstract questions about saints with a direct, personal test. It applies to strangers, but it is harder for those inside your house because familiarity numbs us. The author will also note that opposing someone or refusing them is still possible; the rule is not to be kind to everyone.

The essay will permit force only when gentler means fail and someone is being hurt. It will forbid humiliating others for pleasure, treating children as fair game, or dismissing their suffering because you dislike them. The author will frame this as a shared standard: when someone is being diminished in a kitchen, classroom, meeting, or crowd, saying "They are a person. Stop" is not a private scruple but a reminder of something the room already agreed to.

The essay will introduce a rule called **the pause**. It explains that most destructive acts happen in the minutes after insult, fear, or shame, when the body floods and the mind narrows to a single exit. In that narrowness the future disappears. The pause is a practice that everyone can name without shame.

The pause is a concrete rule for moments of intense emotion. When fury, panic, lust, or desperation takes over, the person waits. They do not send a message, raise their hand, make a promise, or issue a threat. They move the body elsewhere and let the blood recede. In that moment it feels like losing, but it is not. The pause is how you stay the person you are when you are not possessed. Anyone who mocks you for taking it is telling you they prefer you impulsive.

The essay will warn that leaders must observe the pause more strictly, because power shortens the distance between a mood and a wound. It will also introduce a second pause: before believing or passing on a story that makes you feel righteous, such as a rumor or tale about "those people," you wait.

The essay will warn that stories have killed more people than most weapons. It will ask who saw the event, whether the tale flatters hatred, and what would happen to an innocent person if it turned out false. The author will note that doubting only stories that insult friends is not enough.

The essay will then turn to repair. It will acknowledge that everyone will fail, including those we love. The question is not whether we will hurt people, but whether the hurt is allowed to harden. Repair is a skill, and most people are bad at it because they were taught to defend their self-image instead.

Repair is a four-part practice. Name the specific act without explanation. Acknowledge the effect on the other person in their terms. Say what you will do differently in an observable way. Then do it. Leave out "if." Leave out the other person's history or your own childhood as justification.

The essay will also address the recipient of a repair. A genuine apology should not be treated as a defeat. People who are punished for apologizing stop apologizing, not stopping their harm. They only stop telling the truth about it. Forgiveness is not the same as trust. You can accept the words and still require changed behavior before you put weight on the relationship again. You can also leave. Repair is an offer, not a trap.

The essay will close with a warning that no one is obliged to stay with a person who hurts them and calls it love. It will also state that abuse of children or anyone's body against their will is not a quarrel but an injury for which the first duty is protection. The vulnerable person must be kept safe, and the one who caused the harm must not be hidden behind loyalty, reputation, or the peace of the household. The author will note that we would each beg for this if we were the small one in the room.

The essay will close with a call to raise children. Every person was once a child, and whatever was done to them in those years is still partly in the room. The single investment that improves the world for the greatest number of people is this: raise your own children, the ones in your care, and to the extent you can, the ones around you. They do not need perfection. They need a few things reliably. They need to be unafraid in their own house.

Children must be unafraid of the people who claim to love them, not of limits. If a child flinches when you reach for a cup, something has already gone wrong; stopping it matters more than winning the dispute that led there.

They need language. Talk to them before they can answer. Tell them what you are doing, what you see, and the names of things. Answer their questions past the point of your convenience. A child who is spoken to learns that the world can be described and that they are worth describing it to.

Children need to attempt things they are bad at without being mocked. Competence is the residue of tolerated failure. Laughter at a child's clumsiness teaches them to avoid learning moments for life. Praise should be specific and true: "You kept going" is better than "you are brilliant." Adults must also apologize.

A child who never sees repair learns that the powerful do not have to account for themselves. That lesson, carried into their own power, is how cruelty travels across generations. You can end the journey in your house.

Do not hit them. This is the part where some readers will feel their own childhood stand up to argue. It will say that you were hit and you turned out fine, or that children are wild and only fear will civilize them, or that your culture has always done it and an essay does not get a vote. Hear it, and then set it down. Fear is not civilization.

Fear teaches a child to hide, lie, and hit when they are the larger one. You can hold a limit without leaving a bruise or a humiliation. You can remove a privilege, stop a pleasure, require a repair, hold a small furious person until the storm passes, and still be the place they run to when the world is worse than you are. If you were hit, you were not fine in the moment you were hit. You survived it. Survival is not the standard we are aiming for. We are aiming for children who do not have to survive their own parents.

Teach them to read if you can, or get them near someone who will.

Reading is the cheapest freedom. It opens every book ever written, including ideas that have not yet reached your village.

When a teenager becomes unbearable, remember the asymmetry: they are still learning how to be a person, while you already know what you are doing. Do not fight them. Win their trust for the decade in which their mistakes grow larger.

You are not excused from this section if you have no children. You were once a child, and you share rooms, roads, and institutions with the people raising children now.

The next generation is the only country everyone will have to live in. You can refuse to mock a struggling parent and also refuse to look away from a child being harmed. You can teach the thing you know.

We cannot cooperate with people we cannot believe. This is not a philosopher's point. It is why the well gets poisoned, why the medicine is fake, why the bridge falls, why the peace talks fail, and why the neighbor's door stays shut. Lies are convenient one at a time. In bulk they are a collapsed society.

The essay will close with a rule for public truth: do not say what you do not believe in any matter where another person will rely on you. Do not certify work you did not do. Do not sell what you know is rotten. Do not sign what you know is false. Do not nod along with a cruelty because contradicting it would cost you status. The small nod is how large lies recruit their armies.

Lies told to protect the innocent from the wicked — such as hiding a guest or giving a false direction to a hunting party — are not violations of this rule.

Truth-telling is in the service of people, not words. In ordinary life, say "I don't know" when you do not, and say "I was wrong" before the story hardens. Distinguish what you saw from what you heard from what you guessed. If your work informs others, correct your errors at the same volume you used to spread them.

Do not demand certainty before acting on what is already clear. "I might be wrong" is a reason to stay humble. It is not a reason to stand still while something obvious burns. We can hold both: enough doubt to listen, enough conviction to move.

If a person is in serious trouble and you can help at small risk and small cost to yourself, you help. You do not negotiate with yourself about whether they are your responsibility. The drowning child is your responsibility because you are the one standing there.

The rescue rule is obvious in theory, yet it breaks down in practice.

In crowds we freeze because each person assumes someone else will act. The cure is specific: do not shout for help. Shout a name or point at a face and give that person the job. If no one else is doing it, the name is yours.

We also walk past slow disasters because they are not cinematic. A child with days of diarrhea does not look like a moral emergency. A person unraveling alone in a room does not look like a fire. They may be.

The easy rescue also covers the unglamorous moments: sitting down, checking, asking, carrying water, and making calls.

We fail because we do not know a few facts that turn helplessness into competence. Learn these and teach them like the location of the well.

A person bleeding heavily needs firm pressure on the wound with cloth, held without peeking every few seconds to see if it worked. They need help coming. If the blood is spraying or will not stop, this is not a moment for tidiness. It is a moment for pressure and speed.

Severe diarrhea can kill from dehydration that looks like thirst. The rescue is oral rehydration: one liter of clean water with six level teaspoons of sugar and half a teaspoon of salt, given in small sips. If the person cannot drink, is listless, has blood in the stool, is an infant, or is getting worse, they need medical care immediately. This drink is not a substitute for care; it is what you do on the way when help is far away.

Wash your hands with soap, especially after using the latrine and before feeding a child or preparing food. This stops illnesses that have killed more people than all the wars you have heard of. It is not manners. It is how you decline to be a carrier of someone else's funeral.

Smoke, given time, ruins lungs, hearts, and the air of everyone in the house, including the child who did not choose it. If you smoke, stopping is one of the largest gifts you can give the people who will be alive when you might not be.

If you do not smoke, do not start. There is no clever version.

Sleep, daylight, and some way of moving your body are not decorations on a life. They are the conditions under which a mind stays fit to do any of the rest of this. A person who has not slept is a worse parent, a worse judge, a worse friend, and a more dangerous driver. Treat the lack of sleep, in yourself and in those you schedule, as a kind of drunkenness.

None of this requires you to become a saint who abandons their own family for distant causes.

If you have more than enough, more than enough is a tool. Used locally or far away, on a neighbor's school fees or a stranger's bed, it is the same virtue: someone else's serious harm mattered more to you than a comfort you will not remember in a year. Keep enough to stay generous next year. The point is not to be poor. The point is that money and time are forms of the easy rescue, stored.

You become what you repeatedly attend to.

The stories you rehearse become the predictions you make. Those predictions shape how you treat people. That treatment shapes your life and the character of your place.

Some industries profit from fear and anger. They hand you a daily ration of enemies. Many are real. Many are enlarged, simplified, or invented. A simple enemy keeps you watching.

You owe the people around you a mind that has not been rented out.

Before you adopt a hatred, ask who is paid if you hate, and whether the person they have described could be walked up to and spoken with. If the hatred cannot survive contact with an actual human being, it was not knowledge. It was fuel.

Keep at least one relationship where you can say what is actually happening to you. Loneliness is not only sadness. It is a health hazard and a judgment hazard. People with no one to correct them drift into private worlds, and private worlds are where both despair and cruelty ripen. If you have that one person, be that person for someone else.

Much of the world's suffering is produced by work done badly or left corrupt. Diluted medicine, walls built without reinforcing bars, grades given for a bribe, and salted fields that would never be tolerated in a garden the worker's own children had to eat from are all examples. You may not be able to fix the system you work in.

You can refuse to be the place where corruption succeeds. Do your central task as if someone you love will live with the result, because someone whom someone loves will live with it. If your job demands cheating, look hard for a way to stop and do not soothe yourself with how many others do it; numbers are not a conscience.

If you have power over other people's working days, remember that contempt is expensive. People humiliated at work spend their evenings paying that humiliation forward into traffic, kitchens, and children.

Dignity is not a luxury good. It is one of the ways a society stops eating itself.

The person in front of you is the test, not the boundary. Beyond them are people you will never meet: the ones downstream of your waste, the ones who will breathe the air you leave, the ones not born. You do not have to solve their lives this afternoon. You do have to refrain from the casual destruction that is only possible because they cannot knock on your door. Do not take, spoil, or burn what you do not need, when the cost will be paid by someone with no voice in the taking.

Soil, water, forests, and a stable climate are not scenery. They are the unborn's only inheritance and the poor's only buffer.

Other animals are not persons in the way a child is a person, but their suffering is real. They flinch. They fear. They prefer not to be hurt. Where you can avoid adding to that hurt at little cost — in what you fund, what you ignore, what you do with an animal in your hands — avoid it.

arguments.content:
# The Person in Front of You

Most of the harm in the world is done by people who believe, in the moment, that they are justified.

Not by the rare monster who enjoys suffering. By the parent who is tired. The official who is owed a favor. The neighbor who heard a story. The driver who is late. The crowd that would rather not go first. They are not plotting a ruin. They are inside a story in which the next act feels necessary, and the person on the receiving end is slightly less real than they are.

A cup is knocked over at the end of a long day. A rumor arrives that flatters your anger. A child looks up to see what adults do when they are insulted. Someone is hurt at the side of the road, and there is a crowd, which means there is a chance that no one will move. A paper is waiting to be signed that says a thing you know is false.

The world is not only made of such minutes. There are storms, prices, microbes, bad laws, and men with armies who do not care what anyone has read. A larger share of human suffering than we like to admit is still manufactured locally, by ordinary people, in moments when they could have done otherwise. This essay is about those moments. It will not make you important. It may make you trustworthy. Trustworthiness is quieter than importance, and it improves the lives of more people.

Everyone else has read this too. That changes what these words are. Advice given to one person is a private resolution, easy to abandon. The same words, known by all, and known to be known by all, become a standard. You may expect this of your neighbor. Your neighbor may expect it of you. What follows is written so we can remind each other without inventing the language each time.

I will not tell you which god to worship, which party deserves you, or which nation is the hero of the story. People who agreed about all three have still destroyed one another. People who agreed about none of them have still kept one another's children alive through a winter. If your tradition already teaches these duties, this is not a rival to it. It is a reminder you can use on the days the tradition is only a word in your mouth. The practices here do not require your side to win. They require you to act like a person among persons when that costs you something.

None of this replaces bread, medicine, a just law, or a state that does not prey on its people. If you are reading this hungry, or in danger, or ground down by work that never ends, you are not the missing kindness the world is waiting on. Take what protects you. Use what fits. Pass the rest to someone with more room.

If you are reading this with room — spare time, spare money, spare safety — then you are the one the hard cases are waiting on. Room is a duty.

## They are as real as you

You have never felt another person's pain. You have felt only your own, and then imagined the rest. This is why you can say a sentence that will ring in someone's skull for twenty years and, a moment later, feel almost nothing. The nerves are yours. The excuse writes itself: I didn't mean it. They are exaggerating. They deserved it. They are not like us. I had a hard day.

The correction is not a feeling. Feelings are weather. The correction is a question you can ask with a closed heart: if the positions were reversed, and the other person had your power, your mood, and your talent for explaining yourself, what would you beg them not to do?

Not "what would a saint do." What would you be unable to bear if you were the small one in the room.

This applies to the stranger. It applies, harder, to the people in your house, because familiarity is a numbness. It applies to the person you are sure is wrong. You may oppose them. You may refuse them. You may stop them by force if they are hurting someone and nothing gentler will work. You may not humiliate them for pleasure, or treat their children as fair game, or decide that their suffering stopped being real on the day you came to dislike them.

Cruelty is often a ladder. People diminish others because an audience will give them status for it: a laugh in a kitchen, a promotion in an office, a following online, a moment of belonging in a crowd. When someone is cruel for spectators, the spectators are part of the act. Withhold the laugh. Do not pass it on. Do not reward it with attention, promotion, or love. A status economy of cruelty collapses when it stops paying. We can collapse it.

There is a line, and we should say it plainly, because euphemism is where this particular harm hides. You do not get to use another person's body against their will. Not for sex. Not for a beating. Not for labor that is slavery. Using a child sexually is among the worst things a human being can do, and protecting the child outranks loyalty, reputation, religion, and the peace of the household. If the person who did it is one of yours, they are still the person who did it. We would each beg for that standard if we were the small one in the room. We have agreed to it now.

The person in front of you is the test, not the whole map. Beyond them are people you will never meet: downstream of your waste, breathing what you leave in the air, not yet born. You do not have to solve their lives this afternoon. You do have to refuse the casual destruction that is only possible because they cannot knock on your door. Soil, water, shade, a stable climate, a road that is safe at night — these are not scenery. They are other people's lives, stored. Do not take, spoil, or burn what you do not need, when the cost will be paid by someone with no voice in the taking.

The other animals are not persons in the way a child is a person. You do not need to pretend they are in order to treat their suffering as real. They flinch. They fear. They try to get away. Where you can avoid adding to that hurt at little cost — in what you pay for, what you ignore, what you do with an animal in your hands — avoid it. Mercy that stops at the edge of our species has always been tempted to stop at the edge of our tribe. Do not smuggle that temptation back in through the barn door.

## The pause

Most of the worst things people do, they do in the minutes after they have been insulted, frightened, or shamed. The body floods. The mind narrows to one exit: strike, scream, send the message, take the swing, reveal the secret, gather the allies and destroy the offender. Inside that narrowness the future disappears. You cannot see the apology you will owe, the child who is watching, the years of mistrust, the injury that does not reverse.

So we adopt a rule, and because everyone knows it, we can name it without shame. Call it the pause.

When you are lit up — furious, panicked, triumphant, hungry to win, wanting someone in a way that forgets they are a someone — you wait. Ten breaths if the act is small. A night if it is large. You do not send the message. You do not raise your hand. You do not make the promise or the threat. You put your body somewhere else and let the blood recede.

This will feel, while it is happening, like losing. It is not losing. The pause is how you remain the person you are when you are not possessed. Anyone who mocks you for taking it prefers you impulsive. That preference is not in your interest, and it is not in anyone else's.

If you are strong, or large, or armed with authority, the pause is not a suggestion. A body that can do damage has a shorter path from mood to wound. Men, especially: the strength you were praised for can ruin a life in a minute you will not be able to undo in a year of regret. The pause is the tax on that strength. Pay it every time. Alcohol makes the tax harder to pay and the excuse easier to offer. If you cannot keep drink small, treat it as a fire in the house — something you do not leave near the people you might hurt.

If you lead others — a family, a crew, a town, a company — you owe them this more, not less. Power shortens the distance between a bad hour and a lasting harm. The more your words weigh, the longer you hold them.

There is a second pause, smaller and just as useful: the pause before you believe. When a story arrives that makes you feel righteous — a rumor, a clipping, a tale of what *those people* did — you wait before you pass it on. Ask who saw it. Ask whether it is the kind of story that flatters your hatred. Ask what would happen to an innocent person if it traveled and turned out false. Stories have killed more people than most weapons. You do not get to call yourself careful if you only doubt the stories that insult your friends.

And there is a third, aimed at the long erosion rather than the sudden blow. You become what you repeatedly look at. The grievances you rehearse become the predictions you make. The predictions become the way you treat people. There are trades — political, commercial, sometimes religious — that are paid when you are afraid. They will hand you a daily ration of enemies. Some of those enemies are real. Many are enlarged or invented, because a simple enemy keeps you watching. Before you adopt a hatred, ask who is paid if you hate, and whether the person they described could be walked up to and spoken with. If the hatred cannot survive contact with an actual human being, it was not knowledge. It was fuel.

## Repair

You will fail the previous pages. So will everyone you love. The question is not whether you will hurt people. It is whether the hurt is allowed to harden into the shape of a life.

Repair is a skill. Most of us are bad at it because we were taught to protect our picture of ourselves instead. A real repair has four parts, and you can check them the way you check a gate:

Name what you did, specifically, without a fog of explanation around it.

Acknowledge the effect in the other person's terms, not yours.

Say what you will do differently, in a way that can be seen.

Then do that thing.

Leave out the word "if." "If you were hurt" is not repair. Leave out the catalogue of their crimes, unless you are having a different conversation, at a different time, about a different wound. Leave out your childhood as a reason they should absorb this one. Reasons can explain. They do not mend.

If you are the one receiving the attempt, do not treat a genuine repair as a defeat. People who are punished for apologizing stop apologizing. They do not stop doing harm. They only stop telling the truth about it. If we want a world in which people can come back from their worst minutes, we have to leave a door open when they actually come back. Forgiveness is not the same as trust. You can accept the words and still wait for the changed behavior before you put weight on the relationship again.

You can also leave.

Repair is an offer, not a trap. No one is obliged to stay with a person who hurts them and calls it love. If someone shows you this essay to argue that you must endure them, they have not understood it. The person in front of them is you.

What does not belong in the doctrine of repair is the abuse of a child, or the use of anyone's body against their will, or a beating, or a campaign of fear. Those are not quarrels. The first duty is protection: get the vulnerable person safe, and do not hide the one who did it behind loyalty or the family's good name. If you are young and someone in your home is hurting you, the aim is a safe adult, not a night alone on the road — another relative, a teacher, a neighbor, a clinic, a person whose job is to listen. Telling is not betrayal. We have already agreed that the small one's safety outranks the peace of the house.

For ordinary failures, learn to apologize while the apology is still cheap. A crack mends cleanly on the day it happens. Left for a year, it becomes the shape of the wall.

## The long work

Every person you will ever meet was once a child, and part of what was done to them in those years is still in the room. If there is a single investment that improves the world for the greatest number of people, it is this: raise the children in your care so that they are safe, spoken to, and not used as vessels for adult rage. The rest of us should make that easier, not harder.

They do not need perfection. They need a few things, reliably.

They need to be unafraid of the people who claim to love them. Not unafraid of limits. Limits are a kindness. A child who never hears no becomes a danger to everyone they will later have power over, including themselves. But they should not be afraid of your hand, your voice, your mood coming through the door. If a child flinches when you reach for a cup, something has already gone wrong. Stop the thing that taught the flinch. Stopping it matters more than winning the dispute that led there.

They need language. Talk to them before they can answer. Tell them what you are doing, the names of things, what you see. Answer their questions past the point of your convenience. A child who is spoken to learns that the world can be described, and that they are worth describing it to. This is how minds are built, in every language, with no equipment but an adult who stays in the conversation.

They need to be bad at things without being mocked. Skill is what remains after tolerated failure. If the people at home laugh when a child is clumsy, the child will spend years avoiding the moments in which a person learns. Praise what is specific and true. "You kept going" teaches more than "you are brilliant." "You told the truth just then" teaches more than "you are a good boy."

They need to see an adult apologize. A child who never sees repair learns that the powerful do not have to account for themselves. Carried into their own power, that lesson is how cruelty travels across generations. You can end the trip in your house.

Do not hit them. Some readers will feel their own childhood stand up to argue. It will say that you were hit and turned out fine, that children are wild and only fear will civilize them, that your people have always done it and an essay does not get a vote. Hear it, and then set it down. Fear is not civilization. Fear teaches a child to hide, to lie, and to hit when they become the larger one. Where people have looked carefully at the results, the children who were hit are not calmer, not more honest, and not better off. You can hold a limit without a bruise and without humiliation. You can remove a privilege, require a repair, pick a small furious person up and wait out the storm, and still be the place they run to when the world is worse than you are. If you were hit, you were not fine in the minute it happened. You survived. Survival is not the standard. The standard is a child who does not have to survive their own parents.

Teach them to read if you can, or get them near someone who will. A person who can read can learn anything else that has been written down, including things their own town does not yet know. There is no cheaper freedom. Do not keep a daughter from it. A girl who learns changes not only her own life but the health and chances of the children she may someday have. Boys need the same learning, and they need something else that many houses still fail to teach them: the work of keeping people alive. Cooking, cleaning, watching the sick, waking in the night with an infant — this is not a hobby that happens to attach to women. It is work. If one person in your house does almost all of it, you are not looking at a law of nature. You are looking at a choice, usually an old one. Boys who are never taught this work grow up to be dependents who think they are masters. Teach them young.

When the children are older and unbearable, which they will be, remember the asymmetry. They are practicing how to be a person. You are already supposed to know. Do not wage war on a teenager to defend your dignity. Dignity that requires a child's defeat is not dignity. Win their trust for the years in which the mistakes get larger.

If you have no children, you are not excused from this section. You were a child. You share roads, rooms, and rules with people raising them. You can refuse to mock a struggling parent, and you can refuse to look away from a child being harmed. You can teach the thing you know. The next generation is the only country everyone will have to live in.

## Truth, and the disagreement that remains

We cannot cooperate with people we cannot believe. This is not a theory. It is why the well gets poisoned, why the medicine is fake, why the bridge falls, why the peace talks fail, why the neighbor's door stays shut. A lie is convenient one at a time. In bulk, lies are a collapsed society.

The rule, which we can now cite to each other: do not say what you do not believe, in any matter where another person will rely on you. Do not certify work you did not do. Do not sell what you know is rotten. Do not sign what you know is false. Do not nod along with a cruelty because contradicting it would cost you standing. The small nod is how large lies recruit their armies.

There are lies told to protect the innocent from people who would harm them — the hidden guest, the false direction given to the hunting party. Those are not violations of this rule. They are the rule, applied to the person who will rely on you most desperately. Truth is in the service of people, not in the service of words for their own sake.

For the rest of ordinary life, the discipline is plain. Say "I don't know" when you don't. Say "I was wrong" when you were, promptly, before the false version has hardened into something you must defend. Distinguish what you saw from what you heard from what you guessed. If your work is to inform others — teacher, journalist, official, friend in a crowded conversation — your errors are not private. Correct them at the same volume you used to spread them.

Keeping your word is the same virtue, stretched over time. Do not promise what you will not do. A place where promises are casual is a place where everyone must add a tax of suspicion to every plan. That tax is paid by the poor first, because they have no spare to cover someone else's unreliability.

You will still disagree with people who have read every word of this. Good. A world that agrees about everything has stopped looking.

When you dispute, dispute the claim. Do not dispute the human being's right to be in the room. Describe the strongest version of their view, not the stupidest one you can hang around their neck — if only because you cannot answer a position you have misdescribed, and everyone watching can tell. Ask one question you do not already know the answer to. If you cannot, you are not in a disagreement. You are in a performance.

Some disagreements are about facts, and facts are not a courtesy. Someone is wrong about the dose, the date, the boundary, the culprit. Say so plainly. Correcting an error is not arrogance when you have looked and they have not. It is a form of rescue. Do it without an audience when the goal is to change a mind. Public shame makes people defend the error in order to defend themselves. Save the public word for harm that is happening now and needs to be stopped.

Some disagreements are about the shape of a good life, and will not end tonight. You can share a well, a street, a workshop, and a country with a person whose picture of the good is not yours, so long as both of you keep the earlier limits: they are a person, the pause holds, the small are not fair game, and no one is forced to live inside a lie. Peace is not the product of consensus. Peace is the product of limits.

Do not make a spouse, a friend, or a colleague pass a test of total agreement. People who require this end up surrounded by liars, and then they are surprised.

"I might be wrong" is a reason to listen. It is not a reason to stand still while something obvious burns. Hold both. Enough doubt to learn. Enough conviction to move.

## The easy rescue

Some duties are heavy. This one is not, and failing it is still how a great deal of dying happens.

If a person is in serious trouble, and you can help at small risk and small cost, you help. You do not open a negotiation with yourself about whether they are your kind. You are the one standing there. That is the whole argument.

Everyone agrees with this in the abstract. We fail in a few predictable ways.

We freeze in crowds, because each person assumes another will act. Do not shout "someone call for help." Point at a face, give that person the job, and if no one else is doing it, the person is you.

We walk past slow disasters because they are not bright enough to look like emergencies. A child on the third day of diarrhea does not look like a moral crisis. They are one. The unglamorous rescue counts: sit down, check, ask, carry the water, make the call, stay until it is done.

We also fail by not knowing a few facts that turn helplessness into competence. Learn them, and teach them, the way you would teach the location of the well.

A person who is bleeding heavily needs firm, continuous pressure on the wound, with cloth, held without lifting every few seconds to see if it worked. If something is stuck in the wound, do not pull it out. Press around it. Get help coming. This is not a moment for tidiness.

A sudden droop in the face, weakness in an arm, or speech that will not come out right is an emergency of minutes, not of "let's see in the morning." So is sudden pressure in the chest, especially with sweat, nausea, or pain traveling into the arm or jaw. So is heavy bleeding after a birth — pad after pad, faintness, a woman going pale. Do not leave her. Get the most skilled person you can reach, now.

A person losing water to severe diarrhea can die of a problem that looks like tiredness and thirst. If you have proper oral rehydration packets, use them; they are better than a homemade drink. If you do not, and help is far, this is the recipe that has saved more children than most famous medicines: one liter of clean water, six level teaspoons of sugar, half a level teaspoon of salt. Stir until it dissolves. It should not taste saltier than tears. If it does, throw it out and start again; too much salt is dangerous. Give it in small sips, steadily. Keep feeding. Keep breastfeeding. If the person cannot drink, vomits everything, has blood in the stool, is listless or hard to wake, is an infant, or is getting worse, this drink is what you do on the way to skilled care. It is not a reason to stay home. The World Health Organization keeps a plain account of diarrheal disease and why replacing fluids quickly matters: [Diarrhoeal disease](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/diarrhoeal-disease).

Hands washed with soap, after the latrine and before preparing food or feeding a child, cut off illnesses that still kill children in large numbers. This is not manners. It is how you decline to carry someone else's funeral on your fingers.

Smoke, given time, ruins lungs and hearts, and it ruins the air of everyone in the house, including the child who did not choose it. If you smoke, stopping is one of the largest gifts you can give the people who expect you to still be here. If you do not smoke, do not start. There is no clever version of this fact.

Diseases that used to fill graveyards with children can now be stopped before they start. The fear of a needle is older and louder than the memory of those graveyards, which is why the fear sometimes wins. Unless a clinician has a specific reason for this particular child, vaccination is part of the easy rescue. Do not leave a child unprotected against a harm we already know how to prevent. If you are unsure, ask a clinician, not a rumor.

Sleep, daylight, and some way of moving your body are not decorations. They are the conditions under which a mind stays fit for any of the rest of this. A person who has not slept is a worse parent, a worse judge, a worse friend, and a more dangerous driver. Treat a serious lack of sleep, in yourself and in the people whose hours you control, as a kind of drunkenness.

And do not be the disaster yourself. Speed, alcohol, and a phone in the hand kill strangers who were doing everything right. An open flame near a sleeping child is not a small risk in a house of cloth and wood. Their families will not be comforted that you were in a hurry, or that you had always done it that way before.

None of this requires you to abandon your own to become a saint of distant causes. It requires you to stop stepping over the rescue that is already within reach. If you have more than enough, more than enough is a tool. Used on a neighbor's school fees or on a stranger's bed net, it is the same virtue: someone else's serious harm mattered more to you than a comfort you will not remember next year. Keep enough to stay generous next year. The point is not to become poor. The point is that money and time are the easy rescue, stored.

One relationship belongs in this section, because it saves lives without looking like rescue. Keep at least one person to whom you can say what is actually happening to you. Loneliness is not only sadness. It clouds judgment, and it is where despair ripens. If you have that one person, be that person for someone else.

## The work

A great deal of the world's suffering is produced by work done badly, and by work left corrupt. The medicine diluted. The wall built without what the wall needs. The grade, the license, or the verdict given because a hand was paid or a relative asked. The lesson skipped. The pump "fixed" so that it fails next week and must be paid for again.

You may not be able to repair the system you work in. You can refuse to be the point at which it fails. Do the central part of your job as if someone you love will have to live with the result, because someone whom someone loves will have to live with the result.

Honesty is more complicated for the person being squeezed than for the person doing the squeezing, and it is a lie to pretend otherwise. If you are extorted — the checkpoint, the clerk who will not file the paper, the gate between your child and a surgery — protecting the vulnerable person in your care comes first. Pay if you must to get them through, and do not call yourself wicked for it. Then, when it is safe, tell the truth about the extortion. Silence is what the extortionist is buying.

If you are the one who demands the envelope, you are not in that story. You are the reason the story exists. So is the seller who dilutes the milk, the builder who skips the part of the wall no one will see, the colleague who certifies a safety they did not check. "Everyone does it" is not a conscience. It is a description of how a place becomes unlivable. Numbers do not absolve the person who still has a choice. And almost everyone in that chain still has a choice about the powerless person at the end of it. Do not cheat the person who cannot punish you. That is the minimum.

If your job requires you to cheat people as its ordinary purpose, look hard for a way out, and while you are still in it, do the least harm the job allows and do not soothe yourself with the uniform, the quota, or the rent.

If you have power over other people's working days, remember that contempt is expensive. People who are humiliated at work spend the evening paying that humiliation forward, into traffic, into kitchens, into children. Dignity is not a luxury good. It is one of the ways a society stops eating itself. Correct in private. Praise what is specifically true. Do not make anyone beg for the wages or the courtesy you already owe them.

Whatever you know that keeps people alive or free — a crop, a pump, a safe birth, a contract, a rehydration drink, the reading of a page — teach it to two other people. Knowledge locked in one head is a second poverty.

## What we can now expect

Because everyone has read this, a few sentences can be said out loud, and the person who hears them will know what they mean.

*Take the pause.*

*They are a person. Stop.*

*Repair it, or do not pretend it is repaired.*

*Not to the child. Not in front of the child. Not by the child.*

*Did you see it, or did you hear it?*

*That is an easy rescue. Do it.*

*Who is paid if I am afraid?*

Say them the way you would say that the bridge is out. They are not piety. They are information about how we have agreed to live.

You will not feel ready. Readiness was never the entrance requirement. The entrance requirement is the next hour. In it, you will be with someone, or with the consequences of how you treat people when they are absent. You will be tempted to hurry, to win, to look away, to pass on the delicious story, to make a smaller person absorb your mood. That hour is not a prelude to the life in which you become good. It is the life.

The world improves when enough people can be trusted on an ordinary Tuesday: to tell the truth about small things, to spare the people who cannot strike back, to fix what they broke, to do the work as if a stranger's child depended on it, to keep a little of their attention uncaptured by rage. No law can substitute for this. Every decent law depends on it. Institutions are only habits that learned to outlast a single generation. If we keep these habits, our children inherit something sturdier than our opinions. They inherit a place where a person can expect to be treated as real.

That is the work. It is not glorious. It is better than glorious, because it can be done before night, wherever you are, with whatever you have.

Begin with the person in front of you.

# The Person in Front of You

Most of the harm in the world is done by people who believe, in the moment, that they are justified.

Not by the rare monster who enjoys suffering. By the parent who is tired. The official who is owed a favor. The neighbor who heard a story. The driver who is late. The crowd that would rather not go first. They are not plotting a ruin. They are inside a story in which the next act feels necessary, and the person on the receiving end is slightly less real than they are.

A cup is knocked over at the end of a long day. A rumor arrives that flatters your anger. A child looks up to see what adults do when they are insulted. Someone is hurt at the side of the road, and there is a crowd, which means there is a chance that no one will move. A paper is waiting to be signed that says a thing you know is false.

The world is not only made of such minutes. There are storms, prices, microbes, bad laws, and men with armies who do not care what anyone has read. A larger share of human suffering than we like to admit is still manufactured locally, by ordinary people, in moments when they could have done otherwise. This essay is about those moments. It will not make you important. It may make you trustworthy. Trustworthiness is quieter than importance, and it improves the lives of more people.

Everyone else has read this too. That changes what these words are. Advice given to one person is a private resolution, easy to abandon. The same words, known by all, and known to be known by all, become a standard. You may expect this of your neighbor. Your neighbor may expect it of you. What follows is written so we can remind each other without inventing the language each time.

I will not tell you which god to worship, which party deserves you, or which nation is the hero of the story. People who agreed about all three have still destroyed one another. People who agreed about none of them have still kept one another's children alive through a winter. If your tradition already teaches these duties, this is not a rival to it. It is a reminder you can use on the days the tradition is only a word in your mouth. The practices here do not require your side to win. They require you to act like a person among persons when that costs you something.

None of this replaces bread, medicine, a just law, or a state that does not prey on its people. If you are reading this hungry, or in danger, or ground down by work that never ends, you are not the missing kindness the world is waiting on. Take what protects you. Use what fits. Pass the rest to someone with more room.

If you are reading this with room — spare time, spare money, spare safety — then you are the one the hard cases are waiting on. Room is a duty.

## They are as real as you

You have never felt another person's pain. You have felt only your own, and then imagined the rest. This is why you can say a sentence that will ring in someone's skull for twenty years and, a moment later, feel almost nothing. The nerves are yours. The excuse writes itself: I didn't mean it. They are exaggerating. They deserved it. They are not like us. I had a hard day.

The correction is not a feeling. Feelings are weather. The correction is a question you can ask with a closed heart: if the positions were reversed, and the other person had your power, your mood, and your talent for explaining yourself, what would you beg them not to do?

Not "what would a saint do." What would you be unable to bear if you were the small one in the room.

This applies to the stranger. It applies, harder, to the people in your house, because familiarity is a numbness. It applies to the person you are sure is wrong. You may oppose them. You may refuse them. You may stop them by force if they are hurting someone and nothing gentler will work. You may not humiliate them for pleasure, or treat their children as fair game, or decide that their suffering stopped being real on the day you came to dislike them.

Cruelty is often a ladder. People diminish others because an audience will give them status for it: a laugh in a kitchen, a promotion in an office, a following online, a moment of belonging in a crowd. When someone is cruel for spectators, the spectators are part of the act. Withhold the laugh. Do not pass it on. Do not reward it with attention, promotion, or love. A status economy of cruelty collapses when it stops paying. We can collapse it.

There is a line, and we should say it plainly, because euphemism is where this particular harm hides. You do not get to use another person's body against their will. Not for sex. Not for a beating. Not for labor that is slavery. Using a child sexually is among the worst things a human being can do, and protecting the child outranks loyalty, reputation, religion, and the peace of the household. If the person who did it is one of yours, they are still the person who did it. We would each beg for that standard if we were the small one in the room. We have agreed to it now.

The person in front of you is the test, not the whole map. Beyond them are people you will never meet: downstream of your waste, breathing what you leave in the air, not yet born. You do not have to solve their lives this afternoon. You do have to refuse the casual destruction that is only possible because they cannot knock on your door. Soil, water, shade, a stable climate, a road that is safe at night — these are not scenery. They are other people's lives, stored. Do not take, spoil, or burn what you do not need, when the cost will be paid by someone with no voice in the taking.

The other animals are not persons in the way a child is a person. You do not need to pretend they are in order to treat their suffering as real. They flinch. They fear. They try to get away. Where you can avoid adding to that hurt at little cost — in what you pay for, what you ignore, what you do with an animal in your hands — avoid it. Mercy that stops at the edge of our species has always been tempted to stop at the edge of our tribe. Do not smuggle that temptation back in through the barn door.

## The pause

Most of the worst things people do, they do in the minutes after they have been insulted, frightened, or shamed. The body floods. The mind narrows to one exit: strike, scream, send the message, take the swing, reveal the secret, gather the allies and destroy the offender. Inside that narrowness the future disappears. You cannot see the apology you will owe, the child who is watching, the years of mistrust, the injury that does not reverse.

So we adopt a rule, and because everyone knows it, we can name it without shame. Call it the pause.

When you are lit up — furious, panicked, triumphant, hungry to win, wanting someone in a way that forgets they are a someone — you wait. Ten breaths if the act is small. A night if it is large. You do not send the message. You do not raise your hand. You do not make the promise or the threat. You put your body somewhere else and let the blood recede.

This will feel, while it is happening, like losing. It is not losing. The pause is how you remain the person you are when you are not possessed. Anyone who mocks you for taking it prefers you impulsive. That preference is not in your interest, and it is not in anyone else's.

If you are strong, or large, or armed with authority, the pause is not a suggestion. A body that can do damage has a shorter path from mood to wound. Men, especially: the strength you were praised for can ruin a life in a minute you will not be able to undo in a year of regret. The pause is the tax on that strength. Pay it every time. Alcohol makes the tax harder to pay and the excuse easier to offer. If you cannot keep drink small, treat it as a fire in the house — something you do not leave near the people you might hurt.

If you lead others — a family, a crew, a town, a company — you owe them this more, not less. Power shortens the distance between a bad hour and a lasting harm. The more your words weigh, the longer you hold them.

There is a second pause, smaller and just as useful: the pause before you believe. When a story arrives that makes you feel righteous — a rumor, a clipping, a tale of what *those people* did — you wait before you pass it on. Ask who saw it. Ask whether it is the kind of story that flatters your hatred. Ask what would happen to an innocent person if it traveled and turned out false. Stories have killed more people than most weapons. You do not get to call yourself careful if you only doubt the stories that insult your friends.

And there is a third, aimed at the long erosion rather than the sudden blow. You become what you repeatedly look at. The grievances you rehearse become the predictions you make. The predictions become the way you treat people. There are trades — political, commercial, sometimes religious — that are paid when you are afraid. They will hand you a daily ration of enemies. Some of those enemies are real. Many are enlarged or invented, because a simple enemy keeps you watching. Before you adopt a hatred, ask who is paid if you hate, and whether the person they described could be walked up to and spoken with. If the hatred cannot survive contact with an actual human being, it was not knowledge. It was fuel.

## Repair

You will fail the previous pages. So will everyone you love. The question is not whether you will hurt people. It is whether the hurt is allowed to harden into the shape of a life.

Repair is a skill. Most of us are bad at it because we were taught to protect our picture of ourselves instead. A real repair has four parts, and you can check them the way you check a gate:

Name what you did, specifically, without a fog of explanation around it.

Acknowledge the effect in the other person's terms, not yours.

Say what you will do differently, in a way that can be seen.

Then do that thing.

Leave out the word "if." "If you were hurt" is not repair. Leave out the catalogue of their crimes, unless you are having a different conversation, at a different time, about a different wound. Leave out your childhood as a reason they should absorb this one. Reasons can explain. They do not mend.

If you are the one receiving the attempt, do not treat a genuine repair as a defeat. People who are punished for apologizing stop apologizing. They do not stop doing harm. They only stop telling the truth about it. If we want a world in which people can come back from their worst minutes, we have to leave a door open when they actually come back. Forgiveness is not the same as trust. You can accept the words and still wait for the changed behavior before you put weight on the relationship again.

You can also leave.

Repair is an offer, not a trap. No one is obliged to stay with a person who hurts them and calls it love. If someone shows you this essay to argue that you must endure them, they have not understood it. The person in front of them is you.

What does not belong in the doctrine of repair is the abuse of a child, or the use of anyone's body against their will, or a beating, or a campaign of fear. Those are not quarrels. The first duty is protection: get the vulnerable person safe, and do not hide the one who did it behind loyalty or the family's good name. If you are young and someone in your home is hurting you, the aim is a safe adult, not a night alone on the road — another relative, a teacher, a neighbor, a clinic, a person whose job is to listen. Telling is not betrayal. We have already agreed that the small one's safety outranks the peace of the house.

For ordinary failures, learn to apologize while the apology is still cheap. A crack mends cleanly on the day it happens. Left for a year, it becomes the shape of the wall.

## The long work

Every person you will ever meet was once a child, and part of what was done to them in those years is still in the room. If there is a single investment that improves the world for the greatest number of people, it is this: raise the children in your care so that they are safe, spoken to, and not used as vessels for adult rage. The rest of us should make that easier, not harder.

They do not need perfection. They need a few things, reliably.

They need to be unafraid of the people who claim to love them. Not unafraid of limits. Limits are a kindness. A child who never hears no becomes a danger to everyone they will later have power over, including themselves. But they should not be afraid of your hand, your voice, your mood coming through the door. If a child flinches when you reach for a cup, something has already gone wrong. Stop the thing that taught the flinch. Stopping it matters more than winning the dispute that led there.

They need language. Talk to them before they can answer. Tell them what you are doing, the names of things, what you see. Answer their questions past the point of your convenience. A child who is spoken to learns that the world can be described, and that they are worth describing it to. This is how minds are built, in every language, with no equipment but an adult who stays in the conversation.

They need to be bad at things without being mocked. Skill is what remains after tolerated failure. If the people at home laugh when a child is clumsy, the child will spend years avoiding the moments in which a person learns. Praise what is specific and true. "You kept going" teaches more than "you are brilliant." "You told the truth just then" teaches more than "you are a good boy."

They need to see an adult apologize. A child who never sees repair learns that the powerful do not have to account for themselves. Carried into their own power, that lesson is how cruelty travels across generations. You can end the trip in your house.

Do not hit them. Some readers will feel their own childhood stand up to argue. It will say that you were hit and turned out fine, that children are wild and only fear will civilize them, that your people have always done it and an essay does not get a vote. Hear it, and then set it down. Fear is not civilization. Fear teaches a child to hide, to lie, and to hit when they become the larger one. Where people have looked carefully at the results, the children who were hit are not calmer, not more honest, and not better off. You can hold a limit without a bruise and without humiliation. If you were hit, you were not fine in the minute it happened. You survived. Survival is not the standard. The standard is a child who does not have to survive their own parents.
